questions.stem: In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give women the vote in national elections. The campaign's best-known leader was:
options: Vida Goldstein
Millicent Fawcett
Edith Cowan
Kate Sheppard
questions.explanation: Kate Sheppard organised huge petitions, the last signed by nearly 32,000 women, which helped persuade parliament to pass the Electoral Act 1893. Goldstein and Cowan were Australian campaigners and Fawcett led Britain's constitutional suffragists.

questions.stem: New Zealand women won the vote in 1893. Which right did they still lack until 1919?
options: the right to attend university and gain degrees
the right to stand for election to parliament
the right to vote in local council elections
the right to own property after marriage
questions.explanation: Voting and standing were separate rights. New Zealand women could vote from 1893 but could not stand for the House of Representatives until 1919. By contrast, South Australian women won both rights together in 1894.

questions.stem: The right to vote in Queensland state elections was extended to women in:
questions.explanation: Queensland gave women the state vote in 1905, after the Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902 had given most women the federal vote. Irene Longman became the first woman elected to the Queensland Parliament in 1929.

questions.stem: In 1921 Edith Cowan became the first woman to be:
options: elected to the federal Senate
chosen as an Australian premier
elected to an Australian parliament
appointed to Australia's High Court
questions.explanation: Cowan won a seat in Western Australia's Legislative Assembly in 1921. Women did not enter federal parliament until 1943, when Enid Lyons was elected to the House of Representatives and Dorothy Tangney to the Senate.

questions.stem: Australian women gained the federal vote in 1902, yet no woman entered federal parliament until 1943. Which factor best explains the gap?
options: Women were legally barred from standing until 1943
Women's groups opposed women entering parliament
Federal law required candidates to own large estates
Major parties rarely chose women for winnable seats
questions.explanation: The 1902 Act let women stand as well as vote, and several did, but most stood as independents without party machines behind them. The barrier was political and social rather than legal, which shows the limits of formal rights.

questions.stem: Which statement best compares the two main British suffrage organisations by 1914?
options: The WSPU had far more members, while the NUWSS was banned for its violent methods
Both groups had merged into one militant party under Emmeline Pankhurst by 1906
The NUWSS wanted votes for all adults, while the WSPU opposed women voting at all
The NUWSS had more members; the WSPU won more publicity through militancy
questions.explanation: Millicent Fawcett's suffragists used lawful methods and had a much larger, nationwide membership. Pankhurst's suffragettes were fewer but their window smashing, arson and hunger strikes attracted far more attention, for better and worse.

questions.stem: Why did the British government pass the 'Cat and Mouse Act' in 1913 rather than rely only on force-feeding hunger-striking suffragettes?
options: Force-feeding caused outrage, and it feared prisoners dying as martyrs
The courts had ruled that suffragettes could not legally be held in prison at all
Suffragette leaders had agreed to end militancy if hunger strikers were released
Parliament had already decided to give women the vote and wanted to free all prisoners
questions.explanation: The Act let prisoners weakened by hunger strikes be released and then re-arrested once they recovered. It aimed to deny the WSPU martyrs while avoiding the bad publicity of force-feeding, though critics said it was cruel in its own way.

questions.stem: In the 1918 general election, Constance Markievicz became the first woman elected to the House of Commons, but she never took her seat because she:
options: lost the seat in a recount held after the results were announced
chose instead to lead the suffragettes in their continuing campaign
was a Sinn Féin member, and her party boycotted Westminster
was under 30 and so not legally old enough to sit in the Commons
questions.explanation: Sinn Féin's elected members boycotted Westminster and set up their own assembly in Dublin. The first woman to take a seat in the Commons was Nancy Astor, elected in 1919.

questions.stem: The Representation of the People Act 1918 also gave the vote to almost all men over 21. Why did the government need to reform the franchise in 1918 whatever its view of women's war work?
options: Parliament had been dissolved during the war and could not meet without a new franchise
The Allies required Britain to adopt universal suffrage as a condition of the armistice
Most men had already lost the vote when conscription was introduced in 1916
Under the old residence rules, many returning servicemen would have been unable to vote
questions.explanation: Soldiers away from home failed the residence qualifications, and denying them a vote after the war was politically impossible. Once the franchise had to be redrawn, including women became easier, especially as the pre-war campaign had made the issue unavoidable.

questions.stem: The Equal Franchise Act 1928 in Britain:
options: lowered the voting age for both men and women to 18
gave women the vote on the same terms as men, from age 21
gave women over 30 the vote for the first time ever
allowed women to stand for parliament for the first time
questions.explanation: The 1928 Act ended the age and property differences of 1918, so women could vote from 21 like men. Women could stand for parliament from 1918; the voting age fell to 18 in 1969.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Alice Paul's National Woman's Party in the American suffrage campaign?
options: It rejected a federal amendment and campaigned only state by state
It opposed votes for women in wartime as unpatriotic and divisive
It was the official women's branch of the Democratic Party
It used direct action, including picketing the White House in 1917
questions.explanation: Paul's group borrowed militant tactics from Britain; its 'Silent Sentinels' picketed the White House, and arrested members went on hunger strike. The larger NAWSA under Carrie Chapman Catt used lobbying, and both campaigned for the federal amendment ratified in 1920.

questions.stem: Women's anti-suffrage organisations, such as Britain's Women's National Anti-Suffrage League (1908), argued that:
options: women's influence belonged in the home and community, not national politics
only women who paid income tax should be allowed to stand for parliament
women should have the vote immediately but be barred from public office
militant suffragettes were right but should first win over working men
questions.explanation: Some prominent women believed in 'separate spheres' and claimed most women did not want the vote. Their existence shows that the movement did not speak for all women, a point historians weigh when assessing support for suffrage.

questions.stem: In 1923 Huda Shaarawi, founder of the Egyptian Feminist Union, publicly removed her face veil at a Cairo railway station. Why is this significant for a study of the women's movement?
options: It marked the moment Egyptian women won equal voting rights with men
It was organised by British suffragettes living in colonial Egypt
It shows that the movement in Egypt rejected education for women
It shows a non-Western feminist movement with its own goals and leaders
questions.explanation: Shaarawi's union campaigned for education, legal reform of marriage and political rights in a nationalist context. It warns against treating feminism as only a Western story. Egyptian women did not gain the vote until 1956.

questions.stem: In 1942 the Australian government set up the Women's Employment Board. Its main role was to:
options: guarantee that women would keep their wartime jobs when servicemen came home
set pay for women in jobs previously done by men, often above the female rate
conscript all unmarried women aged 18 to 30 into the armed forces and munitions work
close childcare centres so that married women would return to unpaid home duties
questions.explanation: The board could set rates of up to 100 per cent of the male wage for women in 'men's jobs', though most rulings were below the full male rate. It covered only a small share of women workers; most in traditional women's work stayed on lower rates, and many women lost their jobs to returning men after 1945.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the impact of the Second World War on Australian women?
options: It brought equal pay for all women workers by law from 1942
It widened opportunities, but most gains were treated as temporary
It permanently ended the idea that married women should leave paid work
It had little effect, because women were excluded from the services and war industry
questions.explanation: Women joined the services, worked in munitions and the Land Army, and some won higher pay. But the marriage bar and lower female wage rates stayed, and many women were pushed out of skilled jobs at war's end. Change was real but limited.

questions.stem: Which book, published in 1949, argued that women had been defined as the 'Other' in relation to men?
options: The Second Sex by Simone de Beauvoir
The Feminine Mystique by Betty Friedan
The Female Eunuch by Germaine Greer
A Room of One's Own by Virginia Woolf
questions.explanation: De Beauvoir's work argued that womanhood is shaped by society rather than nature, influencing later feminists. Friedan's book appeared in 1963, Greer's in 1970, and Woolf's essay in 1929.

questions.stem: Critics of Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique (1963), including Black feminists such as bell hooks, argued that it:
options: exaggerated the problems of working women and ignored the lives of suburban housewives
opposed women's entry into paid work and urged them to stay at home
was written for a British audience and had no influence in the United States
centred educated white housewives and overlooked women who had to work
questions.explanation: Friedan's study of unfulfilled college-educated housewives struck a chord, but many working-class and African American women had long worked outside the home from necessity. The criticism foreshadowed debates over which women feminism spoke for.

questions.stem: The US Civil Rights Act of 1964 helped the women's movement because its Title VII:
options: legalised abortion across the United States for the first time
banned discrimination in employment on the basis of sex as well as race
gave women the vote in federal elections in states that still denied it
guaranteed equal pay for work of equal value in every state
questions.explanation: Sex was added to the bill during debate, and the new Equal Employment Opportunity Commission received many complaints from women. Slow enforcement helped prompt the founding of the National Organization for Women in 1966.

questions.stem: Consciousness-raising groups, common in the women's liberation movement from the late 1960s, were:
options: government committees that drafted equal pay laws for parliaments and congresses
university courses that trained women to stand as candidates in elections
trade union branches formed by women to run strikes in clothing factories
small women-only meetings where members found their problems were shared
questions.explanation: Talking about marriage, work, sexuality and housework led many women to see private frustrations as products of social structures. The groups helped spread women's liberation ideas quickly and informally.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes liberal feminism from radical feminism in the second wave?
options: Liberals sought equal rights in institutions; radicals saw patriarchy needing deeper change
Liberal feminists opposed equal pay laws; radical feminists wanted women to leave paid work
Liberal feminists were mainly in Australia; radical feminists were only found in Britain
Liberal feminists rejected all legal reform; radical feminists worked through parliament
questions.explanation: Groups like NOW and the Women's Electoral Lobby worked through law and politics. Radical feminists argued that male dominance ran through family, culture and sexuality, and that reform alone was not enough. Socialist feminists linked women's oppression to capitalism.

questions.stem: The Family Law Act 1975 changed Australian women's lives mainly by:
options: giving married women the right to own property separately from husbands
making it compulsory for mothers to receive custody of children after divorce
requiring the husband's consent before a married woman could work
introducing no-fault divorce on the single ground of irretrievable breakdown
questions.explanation: Divorce could be granted after twelve months' separation without proving fault such as adultery, and the Family Court of Australia was created. Married women's property rights had been won in the colonies in the 19th century.

questions.stem: The 1972 equal pay decision of the Australian Conciliation and Arbitration Commission went further than the 1969 decision by adopting the principle of:
options: a family wage for married men
a single minimum wage for youth
equal pay for work of equal value
equal pay for identical work only
questions.explanation: The 1969 ruling helped mainly women doing the same work as men. The 1972 principle covered work of equal value even in female-dominated jobs, and in 1974 the adult minimum wage was extended to women.

questions.stem: The Supporting Mother's Benefit, introduced by the Whitlam government in 1973, was significant because it:
options: ended the payment of family allowances to fathers rather than mothers
gave single mothers an income without relying on a husband
paid all mothers a wage for housework equal to the male minimum wage
provided free childcare for every working mother in Australia
questions.explanation: The payment covered unmarried and separated mothers who had not been eligible for widows' pensions. It was extended to single fathers in 1977. It reflected the movement's demand that women have economic independence.

questions.stem: In 1973 Gough Whitlam appointed Elizabeth Reid as his adviser on women's affairs. Her appointment is significant because:
options: she was the first woman ever elected to Australia's federal parliament
it ended the need for any further anti-discrimination legislation
she led the strike that won equal pay for women in 1969
it was among the first such posts advising a head of government
questions.explanation: Reid's post marked a new approach of bringing feminists into government, the so-called 'femocrats'. The Whitlam years also brought the Supporting Mother's Benefit (1973) and no-fault divorce under the Family Law Act 1975.

questions.stem: The Affirmative Action (Equal Employment Opportunity for Women) Act 1986 required:
options: all political parties to preselect women for half their winnable seats
women to be paid the full male wage in all female-dominated industries
larger employers and universities to plan to remove barriers to women
every employer to hire equal numbers of men and women in each job
questions.explanation: The Act applied to private employers with 100 or more staff and to higher education institutions, which had to report on their programs. It built on the Sex Discrimination Act 1984, which outlawed discrimination on grounds such as sex, marital status and pregnancy.

questions.stem: In 1972 the US Congress passed the Equal Rights Amendment. Why did it fail to become part of the Constitution?
options: The Supreme Court declared it unconstitutional in Roe v. Wade
Women's groups such as NOW withdrew their support for the amendment
Too few states ratified it in time, amid Phyllis Schlafly's campaign
President Nixon vetoed it, and Congress could not override his veto
questions.explanation: The amendment needed 38 states; it reached 35 before the 1982 deadline. Schlafly's STOP ERA campaign argued it would harm housewives and lead to women being drafted. Constitutional amendments do not go to the president for signature.

questions.stem: In Roe v. Wade (1973), the US Supreme Court:
options: banned sex discrimination at work
recognised a constitutional abortion right
ruled that women could serve on juries
upheld the Equal Rights Amendment
questions.explanation: Roe became a central issue for both the women's movement and its opponents. It was overturned in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization in 2022, which returned abortion law to the states. Sex discrimination at work was banned by the Civil Rights Act 1964.

questions.stem: In 1968 women sewing machinists at Ford's Dagenham plant in England went on strike. Their action is significant because it:
options: ended the marriage bar in British public service
led to the closure of the plant and job losses
helped bring about Britain's Equal Pay Act 1970
won women over 30 the right to vote in Britain
questions.explanation: The machinists protested at being graded as unskilled. Their strike drew national attention to unequal pay, and the Equal Pay Act was passed in 1970, followed by the Sex Discrimination Act 1975.

questions.stem: The United Nations declared 1975 International Women's Year. In 1979 the General Assembly adopted:
options: the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women
the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and its two Covenants
the Convention on the Rights of the Child
the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples
questions.explanation: CEDAW, sometimes called an international bill of rights for women, commits states that ratify it to end discrimination in law and practice. The Universal Declaration dates from 1948, the children's convention from 1989 and the Indigenous declaration from 2007.

questions.stem: Swiss women gained the right to vote in federal elections only in 1971. For a study of the movement, this is most useful as evidence that:
options: the women's movement began in Switzerland well before New Zealand's
Swiss women had refused the vote when it was offered in 1893
voting rights came first in countries that fought in both world wars
progress was uneven, and some long-standing democracies acted very late
questions.explanation: Switzerland extended the vote by referendum of male voters, which delayed change; one canton held out until forced by a court in 1990. International comparison shows that suffrage was not a single, steady march.

questions.stem: The Combahee River Collective, a Black feminist group in Boston, issued a statement in 1977 arguing that:
options: women's oppression was caused entirely by capitalism, so race could be ignored
race, sex, class and sexuality were interlocking oppressions to fight together
the vote was the only goal women needed, so other campaigns distracted from it
Black women should leave the women's movement to support only Black nationalism
questions.explanation: The statement criticised both racism in the white women's movement and sexism in Black nationalist and civil rights groups. Its ideas fed into the later concept of intersectionality, named by Kimberlé Crenshaw in 1989.

questions.stem: After the death in custody of Mahsa Amini in Iran in September 2022, mass protests spread under the slogan 'Woman, Life, Freedom'. For a study of the women's movement, this shows:
options: the end of compulsory veiling in Iran after the first week of protest
women outside the West defying state control of dress and lives
the Iranian government granting women the vote for the first time
Western feminist groups organising protests inside Iran itself
questions.explanation: Amini had been detained by the morality police for allegedly breaching hijab rules. The protests, led largely by women and young people, met harsh repression. Iranian women had voted since 1963.

questions.stem: In October 2012 Prime Minister Julia Gillard gave a parliamentary speech attacking sexism and misogyny that was viewed millions of times worldwide. This is significant to the movement's history because:
options: it marked the first time a woman had been elected to the House of Representatives
it announced the passing of the Sex Discrimination Act through the parliament
it ended the use of the marriage bar in the Commonwealth Public Service
it showed that even a woman in the top office faced sexism, sparking debate
questions.explanation: Gillard, Australia's first female prime minister (2010-2013), turned attention to the treatment of women in public life. The speech became a reference point in later debates. The Sex Discrimination Act dates from 1984 and the marriage bar ended in 1966.

questions.stem: A British postcard of about 1910 shows a husband left at home with crying babies while his wife goes out to a suffrage meeting. As a source, it is most useful as evidence of:
options: opponents' fear that votes for women would upend roles at home
how most British families actually divided household work in 1910
the number of women who attended suffrage meetings each week
the arguments that suffragists used to win support for the vote
questions.explanation: Anti-suffrage propaganda mocked the idea of women in politics by suggesting it would leave men doing 'women's work'. It reveals attitudes and anxieties, not how families actually lived.

questions.stem: A historian uses Emmeline Pankhurst's autobiography My Own Story (1914) as evidence for the suffragette campaign. Which is the main limitation of this source?
options: It was written long after the events by someone who did not take part
It is an official government record that ignores the suffragettes' views
It deals only with the campaign in the United States, not Britain
It was written during the campaign by its leader to justify her methods
questions.explanation: Pankhurst's account is valuable for the WSPU's aims and self-image, but it was written to defend militancy and present the movement favourably. A historian would corroborate it with police records, newspapers and suffragist sources.

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports the view that the second wave achieved more change in law than in everyday life?
options: Women's liberation groups held marches and consciousness-raising meetings across Australia
Germaine Greer's The Female Eunuch became an international bestseller in the early 1970s
The Women's Electoral Lobby surveyed candidates before the 1972 federal election
Equal pay and anti-discrimination laws passed, but women still earned less
questions.explanation: Only the first option compares legal change with outcomes in daily life, which is what the judgement requires. The others show the movement's activity and influence but not how far ordinary women's lives changed.
